few_shot.bad_spl: index=security sourcetype=ids_alert earliest=0 | stats count by signature
few_shot.explanation: The classic zombie: scheduled every 5 minutes, earliest=0 rescans all of retention each run, and the search itself is disabled — still occupying a scheduled-search slot definitionally, invisible until someone audits.
few_shot.good_spl: index=security sourcetype=ids_alert earliest=-24h | stats count by signature

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | stats count by host | appendcols [search index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | stats avg(bytes) by host]
few_shot.explanation: appendcols stitches columns by row position, not a key — different ordering or lengths misalign every value. Computing both aggregates in one pass by the key is correct and cheaper (no second dispatch, no positional risk).
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | stats count avg(bytes) AS avg_bytes by host

few_shot.bad_spl: * | stats count by host
few_shot.explanation: A bare * retrieves everything the platform allows — no lexicon terms to intersect, no bloom elimination. Anchor with index + sourcetype + a term.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=200 | stats count by host

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined earliest=-90d | timechart span=1d count
few_shot.explanation: I/O scales linearly with the window. A 90-day window on a search consumed daily pays a ~13x multiplier over the 7 days that answer the question.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined earliest=-7d | timechart span=1d count

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | collect index=summary
few_shot.explanation: collect has no dedup intelligence — re-running over an already-summarized range duplicates every row. Drive it from one non-overlapping schedule (low).
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | stats count by uri_path

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | dedup clientip | stats count
few_shot.explanation: Without sortby, WHICH event survives dedup is order-dependent and it runs on the SH. stats latest() by the key is deterministic and map-reducible (low).
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | stats latest(_time) AS last by clientip

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=404 | delete
few_shot.explanation: delete is irreversible, frees no disk, and hides data from every search. It never belongs in a scheduled or ad-hoc analytics search — the safe intent is a scoped read. Never installed as a demo search.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=404 | stats count by uri_path

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 daysago=7 | stats count by clientip
few_shot.explanation: daysago= is a legacy modifier documented as valid but slated for removal; the snap-aware earliest/latest form is precise and future-proof (low).
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 earliest=-7d@d latest=now | stats count by clientip

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web | head 1000 | search status=500 | stats count by uri_path
few_shot.explanation: head is centralized streaming — placing it before the status filter drags the unfiltered stream to the search head, then throws most of it away.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web status=500 | head 1000 | stats count by uri_path

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status!=200 | stats count by status
few_shot.explanation: Exclusion (field!=x) can't use the lexicon the way inclusion can — Splunk retrieves candidates then discards them, and != also drops null-field events.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined (status=404 OR status=500) | stats count by status

few_shot.bad_spl: index=* *error* | transaction host | table host, _time, _raw
few_shot.explanation: The on-stage query: three anti-patterns stacked — scan every index, defeat the lexicon with a leading wildcard, then assemble transactions from the unfiltered stream on the search head. The rewrite scopes retrieval and replaces transaction with stats.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status>=500 | stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen count BY host

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | rex field=_raw "(.*)error(.*)fatal(.*)"
few_shot.explanation: Multiple .* in one rex forces backtracking across full _raw for every event. Anchor with negated classes ([^,]+) and extract once into named fields.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | rex field=_raw "error=(?<err>[^,]+)"

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | stats count by clientip, uri
few_shot.explanation: stats by a near-unique field (uri) builds one bucket per value — SH memory scales with cardinality. Aggregate by the dimension you actually report on.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | stats count by status

few_shot.bad_spl: sourcetype=my_source | lookup my_lookup_file D OUTPUTNEW L | eval E=L/T | search A=25 L>100 E>50
few_shot.explanation: The canonical pipeline-order example: A=25 belongs in the base search, L>100 immediately after the lookup that creates L; only E>50 must wait for the eval. Filtering last transforms rows that were always going to be dropped.
few_shot.good_spl: sourcetype=my_source A=25 | lookup my_lookup_file D OUTPUTNEW L | search L>100 | eval E=L/T | search E>50

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web *error* | stats count by status
few_shot.explanation: *error* bypasses the lexicon and bloom filters — every term in every bucket is examined. An anchored field filter restores index-time elimination.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=5* | stats count by status

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | lookup http_status_desc status OUTPUT description | stats count by status
few_shot.explanation: The lookup enriches every raw event, but its output (description) is not used by the stats — so it can move after the aggregation and match a handful of grouped rows instead of every event (low: cost).
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | stats count by status | lookup http_status_desc status OUTPUT description

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | head 50 | map search="search index=app host=$host$"
few_shot.explanation: map dispatches a separate search per input row — a concurrent search storm that skips OTHER scheduled searches. Restructure to one search with a key.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | stats count by host

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined host=web*prod-01 | stats count by status
few_shot.explanation: A wildcard spanning punctuation (host=web*prod-01) fights the segmenter and can silently match differently than intended. Match whole segments or TERM().
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined host="webserver-prod-01" | stats count by status

few_shot.bad_spl: index=app log_level=ERROR | stats count by component
few_shot.explanation: An index filter alone pulls every event class in that index. Adding sourcetype narrows the lexicon walk and downstream extraction (low: advisory).
few_shot.good_spl: index=app sourcetype=app_logs log_level=ERROR | stats count by component

few_shot.bad_spl: index=network 10.1.2.3 | stats count by action
few_shot.explanation: A raw IP is segmented on the dots; TERM(10.1.2.3) matches it as one lexicon term instead of intersecting four segments.
few_shot.good_spl: index=network TERM(10.1.2.3) | stats count by action

few_shot.bad_spl: index=app env=prod ERROR | stats count AS errors | append [search index=app env=prod WARN | stats count AS warns] | append [search index=app env=prod INFO | stats count AS infos]
few_shot.explanation: Each append re-dispatches a search over the same index — three reads where one suffices. conditional aggregation over a single OR'd base search reads the data once.
few_shot.good_spl: index=app env=prod (ERROR OR WARN OR INFO) | stats count(eval(searchmatch("ERROR"))) AS errors count(eval(searchmatch("WARN"))) AS warns count(eval(searchmatch("INFO"))) AS infos

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined NOT * | stats count by status
few_shot.explanation: NOT * combined with an index filter without parentheses evaluates with surprising precedence — wrong results, no error. Parenthesize, or use inclusion.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined (status=404 OR status=500) | stats count by status

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web | table clientip, status, uri_path | search status=404 | stats count by clientip
few_shot.explanation: table mid-pipeline is a transforming command — it centralizes and strips fields before the filter runs. fields (distributable) trims columns without the barrier; better yet, filter first.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web status=404 | stats count by clientip

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | stats count by clientip, status | search status=500
few_shot.explanation: stats before the status filter transforms the entire candidate set on the search head, then throws most of it away. Filter in the base search first.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined status=500 | stats count by clientip

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | rex "a=(?<a>\S+)" | rex "b=(?<b>\S+)" | rex "c=(?<c>\S+)"
few_shot.explanation: Each rex re-reads the source field per event; several in sequence multiply parse passes that one combined pattern would do once (low: cost only).
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | rex "a=(?<a>\S+) b=(?<b>\S+) c=(?<c>\S+)"

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | sort 0 _time | transaction clientip maxspan=30m
few_shot.explanation: A sort barrier stacked in front of the already-expensive transaction — two SH-bound buffering passes; usually a smell that stats is the right tool.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | stats earliest(_time) AS s latest(_time) AS e by clientip

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web | stats count by host, sourcetype
few_shot.explanation: Counting by indexed fields only (host, sourcetype) never needs _raw — tstats answers from tsidx alone, routinely 10-100x faster.
few_shot.good_spl: | tstats count where index=web by host, sourcetype

few_shot.bad_spl: index=auth action=failure [search index=threat_intel | fields src_ip] | stats count by src_ip
few_shot.explanation: The threat-intel subsearch is re-run on every execution and silently capped at 10k results / 60s. A lookup holds the same IOC set with no cap and no per-run dispatch.
few_shot.good_spl: index=auth action=failure [| inputlookup threat_intel_iocs | fields src_ip] | stats count by src_ip

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web | transaction clientip maxspan=30m | stats avg(duration)
few_shot.explanation: transaction assembles sessions in search-head memory and silently drops events past maxopentxn/maxopenevents. stats computes the same session bounds distributably, with no eviction.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web | stats earliest(_time) AS start latest(_time) AS end BY clientip | eval duration=end-start | stats avg(duration)

few_shot.bad_spl: | tstats count from datamodel=Web by sourcetype
few_shot.explanation: tstats over an accelerated data model without an index constraint scans all summary buckets — "it uses tstats so it's fast" is false comfort. Constrain inside where.
few_shot.good_spl: | tstats count from datamodel=Web where index=web by sourcetype

few_shot.bad_spl: index=* error | stats count by host
few_shot.explanation: index=* scans every index in the environment. Naming the index turns a platform-wide crawl into a single-index read.
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined "error" | stats count by host

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web | join clientip [search index=firewall] | stats count by action
few_shot.explanation: join buffers its subsearch on the search head, capped at 50k rows / 60s — then truncates silently. A single pass with stats by the common key reads both datasets once and never truncates.
few_shot.good_spl: (index=web) OR (index=firewall) | stats values(action) AS action dc(index) AS sources BY clientip | where sources=2 | stats count by action

few_shot.bad_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | stats count by clientip | sort -count | head 20
few_shot.explanation: A sort with no explicit count keeps only 10,000 rows and drops the rest before head sees them — the top-N can be computed on the wrong slice (low).
few_shot.good_spl: index=web sourcetype=access_combined | stats count by clientip | sort 20 -count

fragments.ALLTIME_RANGE: ALLTIME_RANGE (All-time search window; severity critical): All-time scheduled searches rescan the entire retention window every run — the canonical scheduled-search resource drain called out in Splunk docs. Risk: Cost grows without bound as data ages in; Cloud admission rules may hard-block, breaking the workflow that depends on the search. Fix: Bound the window (earliest=-24h or the schedule interval); for historical baselines use summary indexing or accelerated data models.
fragments.APPENDCOLS_POSITIONAL: APPENDCOLS_POSITIONAL (appendcols joins by row position; severity medium): appendcols runs its argument as a subsearch (the 50k/60s caps apply) and stitches the columns onto the main results — another indexer round-trip on top of the base search. Risk: appendcols matches by ROW POSITION, not a key. If the two result sets are ordered differently or have different lengths, every value lands on the wrong row — the output is confidently wrong with no error. Fix: Join on an explicit key instead of position: one base search with `stats ... BY key`, or a `lookup`. Reserve appendcols for genuinely positional, equal-length, identically-ordered sets.
fragments.APPEND_PROLIFERATION: APPEND_PROLIFERATION (Repeated append subsearches; severity medium): Each | append [search ...] dispatches another full search — typically re-scanning the same indexes the base search already read. Risk: Each append is also a subsearch with the 10k/60s caps and their silent truncation behavior. Fix: One base search with OR'd scopes plus stats/eval to separate the branches; union when branches are genuinely different datasets.
fragments.APPEND_VS_UNION: APPEND_VS_UNION (append chain where one base search serves; severity low): Appending searches that differ only in a filter re-runs retrieval N times. One base search with OR'd scope plus conditional aggregation (stats count(eval(...))) reads the data once. Risk: Inherits subsearch caps per appended branch. Fix: (index=a cond1) OR (index=a cond2) | stats count(eval(cond1)) AS c1 count(eval(cond2)) AS c2 — or union for genuinely distinct datasets.
fragments.APP_DISABLED: APP_DISABLED (Scheduled inside a disabled app; severity medium): The search is enabled and scheduled, but its app is disabled, so the scheduler never dispatches it; it appears in every inventory as a live search that quietly does nothing. Risk: Alerts in a disabled app are the classic silent gap after an app cleanup: the search is enabled, the alert is configured, and nothing ever fires. Fix: Either re-enable the app on purpose or move the searches that still matter to a live app and remove the rest.
fragments.BARE_STAR: BARE_STAR (Bare * retrieval; severity high): A bare * retrieves everything the platform allows — no lexicon terms to intersect, no bloom filter elimination. Risk: Result volume is bounded only by platform limits, so behavior degrades unpredictably as data grows. Fix: Anchor with index, sourcetype, and at least one indexed term before any wildcard.
fragments.BETTER_ALTERNATIVE: BETTER_ALTERNATIVE (Cheaper equivalent exists; severity info): Remediation umbrella used in critique output when a rewrite exists: stats by common key, lookup for reference data, single base search with OR plus stats, accelerated data model via tstats. Risk: Advisory only — carries the rewrite suggestion, not a finding of its own. Fix: Emitted alongside a detector code; the suggested_spl field carries the concrete rewrite.
fragments.BROAD_TIME_RANGE: BROAD_TIME_RANGE (Broader time range than needed; severity medium): I/O scales linearly with the time window. A -30d window when -24h answers the question is a 30x multiplier on every downstream cost. Risk: Long windows on scheduled searches push runDuration toward the cron interval — the self-overlap skip pattern. Fix: Match the window to the question; for scheduled searches, size earliest to the schedule interval plus a safety margin.
fragments.COLLECT_DUPLICATION: COLLECT_DUPLICATION (collect duplicates the summary index on re-run; severity low): collect writes results into a summary index — legitimate for scheduled summary indexing, but it has no dedup intelligence. Risk: Re-running collect over a source/time range it already summarized duplicates every row (community reports of >100x inflation), and it uses the original _time so duplicates scatter historically — every downstream report built on the summary is silently inflated. Safe only when scheduled once per non-overlapping window. Fix: Drive collect from a single, non-overlapping scheduled search; never backfill by re-running it ad hoc over a window already summarized. Prefer data-model acceleration where it fits.
fragments.COMPLEX_REGEX: COMPLEX_REGEX (Greedy regex over _raw; severity medium): Multiple .* in one pattern forces backtracking across full _raw for every event — CPU cost that distributable placement cannot hide. Risk: Pathological backtracking can dominate a search's CPU on hostile input. Fix: Anchor patterns, replace .* with bounded or negated classes ([^"]*), and extract once into fields rather than re-matching.
fragments.DEDUP_VS_STATS: DEDUP_VS_STATS (dedup where stats latest()/values() serves; severity low): dedup keeps arbitrary representatives unless paired with sortby (its non-streaming, expensive mode). stats latest()/values() by key states the intent and aggregates distributably where possible. Risk: Without sortby, WHICH event survives dedup is order-dependent — subtly nondeterministic results. Fix: | stats latest(status) AS status latest(_time) AS _time BY host — instead of | dedup host.
fragments.DELETE_COMMAND: DELETE_COMMAND (delete is irreversible and frees no disk; severity critical): delete marks events unsearchable across the whole environment; it does NOT reclaim disk — the data stays on disk, just hidden from every search. Risk: Irreversible: recovery means re-indexing the source. A too-broad base search silently masks huge swaths of data from all users. A flagged risky command gated behind the can_delete role — its presence in a saved search warrants review every single time. Fix: Do not delete from a scheduled or ad-hoc search. To remove data use index retention (frozenTimePeriodInSecs) or `splunk clean` on a rebuildable index; to hide a subset, fix the upstream filter — never delete.
fragments.DEPRECATED_TIME_MODIFIER: DEPRECATED_TIME_MODIFIER (Deprecated time modifier; severity low): Legacy modifiers (daysago=, startminutesago=, searchtimespanhours=, starttimeu=) are documented as valid but slated for removal, and each is a slower, less flexible path than the relative-time syntax. Risk: Removal risk: a future release drops them and the saved search silently breaks. Correctness-adjacent — they express windows less precisely than snap-aware earliest/latest. Fix: Use earliest/latest with relative units and snapping: daysago=7 becomes earliest=-7d@d latest=now; searchtimespanhours=1 becomes a matched earliest/latest pair.
fragments.DISABLED_BUT_SCHEDULED: DISABLED_BUT_SCHEDULED (Disabled search that still carries a schedule; severity medium): Costs nothing today, but the cron and dispatch window are still set, so a bulk enable, an app update, or a well-meaning admin resurrects it exactly as it was, window and all. Risk: A schedule that outlived its intent: nobody decided this search should run every five minutes over all time, it just never got deleted. Fix: Decide: delete the search, or re-enable it deliberately with a window sized to its interval and an owner who wants its output.
fragments.EARLY_CENTRALIZED: EARLY_CENTRALIZED (Centralized command before filtering; severity high): Centralized streaming commands (transaction, head, streamstats) force all events matched so far onto the search head. Placed before narrow filters, the SH holds an unscoped event set — the map-reduce model inverted. Risk: Search head memory pressure affects every user on the SH, not just the offending search. Fix: Move every distributable filter (search terms, where, fields) ahead of the first centralized command; often the centralized command itself can become stats.
fragments.EMPTY_REPORT: EMPTY_REPORT (Scheduled report nobody and nothing consumes; severity medium): No alert action, no summary index, and 95% or more of its runs return zero results over the measured window: every dispatch pays the scan and the scheduler slot for an answer that is empty and that no downstream consumer would receive anyway. Risk: Either the condition it looks for no longer occurs, or the search is wrong and would miss it if it did; from the outside the two look identical. Fix: Confirm what the report was for. If it fed a dashboard or a person, wire that consumer explicitly; if nothing consumes it, disable it and keep the SPL in version control instead of the scheduler.
fragments.EVENTSTATS_MEMORY: EVENTSTATS_MEMORY (eventstats/streamstats drop columns at the memory cap; severity low): Both buffer aggregation state on the search head across the whole result set — centralized, not distributable to the indexers. Risk: At max_mem_usage_mb (default 200 MB for these) the processor STOPS adding the computed fields to results rather than spilling to disk the way stats does — the column silently goes missing on large sets. Fix: Reduce the set before the windowed stat (filter early, `fields` down), or use `stats` (which spills to disk) when a global aggregate — not a per-event running value — is what you actually need.
fragments.EXCLUSION_PATTERN: EXCLUSION_PATTERN (Exclusion filter in base search; severity medium): Exclusion (NOT field=x, field!=x) cannot use the lexicon the way inclusion can — Splunk still retrieves candidates and discards them. Risk: != also drops events where the field is absent, which is frequently not what the author intended. Fix: Express what you DO want: enumerate the included values, or filter after retrieval with | where when exclusion is genuinely needed.
fragments.GROWING_RUNTIME: GROWING_RUNTIME (Runtime trending up toward the interval; severity medium): Average runtime rose 50% or more between the first and second half of the measured window, the signature of a search whose cost scales with data volume rather than with the interval it is supposed to cover. Risk: On its current trajectory the search meets its own cron interval and starts skipping itself; the failure arrives on the busiest day. Fix: Bound the window to the interval, push filtering to retrieval, or move the rolling computation to summary indexing so each run reads only new data.
fragments.HEAVY_KV: HEAVY_KV (Heavy search-time field extraction; severity medium): High command.search.kv means the search pays per-event extraction cost (KV_MODE, search-time props) across the scanned set — often alongside missing early filters. Risk: Cost signal only. Fix: Filter on indexed fields first; trim with fields; consider indexed extractions for hot sourcetypes.
fragments.HEAVY_LOOKUPS: HEAVY_LOOKUPS (Heavy automatic lookup enrichment; severity medium): High command.search.lookups means automatic lookups are applied to every event scanned — large lookup files multiply the effect. Risk: Cost signal only. Fix: Scope the search so fewer events flow through enrichment; disable unneeded automatic lookups; enrich after aggregation where possible.
fragments.HEAVY_TYPER: HEAVY_TYPER (Heavy eventtype/tag annotation; severity low): High command.search.typer means eventtype and tag evaluation is applied per event — environments with many broad eventtypes pay this on every search that touches them. Risk: Cost signal only. Fix: Constrain eventtype definitions; avoid tag= filters over broad scopes; filter on indexed terms first.
fragments.HIGH_CARDINALITY_BY: HIGH_CARDINALITY_BY (Aggregation by ultra-high-cardinality field; severity medium): stats ... by a near-unique field builds one bucket per event — SH memory scales with cardinality and renders crawl. Risk: Commands capped by max_mem_usage_mb silently limit output when the bucket table exceeds the cap. Fix: Aggregate by the dimension you actually report on; bucket continuous values first (bin); use estdc() for distinct counts.
fragments.HYPERACTIVE_SCHEDULE: HYPERACTIVE_SCHEDULE (Every-minute schedule; severity medium): A */1 cron occupies a scheduler slot 1,440 times a day; few detections genuinely need sub-5-minute latency, and dense schedules crowd out every other search on the host. Risk: Any runtime hiccup immediately self-overlaps; skip storms follow. Fix: Widen to */5 or more; if near-real-time latency is a hard requirement, consider an accelerated data model or streaming-style detection instead.
fragments.JOIN_OVERUSE: JOIN_OVERUSE (join with unbounded subsearch; severity high): join is SH-only and runs its right side as a subsearch — capped at 50k rows (subsearch_maxout join context) and 60s (subsearch_maxtime). SQL habits port badly: Splunk joins buffer and match on the search head. Risk: Past the caps Splunk truncates silently — the canonical log line is "50000 results, truncating to maxout". The join completes, the answer is wrong, nobody is told. Fix: Restructure as a single pass: (index=a) OR (index=b) | stats values(...) by join_key — or use lookup for reference data.
fragments.LATE_FILTER: LATE_FILTER (Movable filter placed late in the pipeline; severity medium): A search/where predicate that only references fields available earlier could have dropped rows before they were transformed or shipped to the SH. The canonical example: | lookup | eval | search A=25 L>100 — A=25 belongs in the base search, L>100 right after the lookup. Risk: Low correctness risk; wasted compute and latency. Fix: Move each predicate to the earliest stage where its fields exist; only predicates on derived fields stay after the eval that derives them.
fragments.LEADING_WILDCARD: LEADING_WILDCARD (Leading wildcard; severity high): Leading wildcards (*fail, field=*value) bypass the tsidx lexicon AND bloom filters — every term in every bucket must be examined. Trailing wildcards (fail*) can still enumerate the lexicon. Risk: Forces the search from dense toward super-sparse on the density spectrum; a single leading-wildcard search can dominate indexer I/O. Fix: Anchor the term: status=fail* instead of *fail*; exact terms or TERM() for tokens; lookup/inputlookup for large ID sets.
fragments.LOOKUP_BEFORE_AGG: LOOKUP_BEFORE_AGG (lookup enrichment before aggregation; severity low): A lookup runs per event on every row that reaches it. When its output fields are not used by the following transforming command, the enrichment could run AFTER the aggregation — matching a handful of grouped rows instead of every raw event. Risk: Cost only. Splunk's own lookup docs give the canonical example: ... | stats count by status | lookup status_desc status OUTPUT description beats doing the lookup before the stats. Fix: Move the lookup after the transforming command when its output is not part of the group-by or aggregation: ... | stats count by <key> | lookup ... <key> OUTPUT <fields>.
fragments.MACRO_OPACITY: MACRO_OPACITY (Search calls macros the critic cannot see inside; severity info): Macros expand before the search runs; SPL Critic analyzes the TEXT, so it cannot see inside a `macro` call. A macro can hide any anti-pattern — index=*, all-time, leading wildcards, join, or summariesonly=false (the ES security_content_summariesonly case expands to raw-data scans through two layers of macro). Risk: Not a defect — an audit-coverage gap. A clean verdict on a macro-heavy search is only as complete as the macros are benign. Fix: Expand the search to audit it fully — Search preview (Cmd/Ctrl-Shift-E) or `splunk btool macros list` — then re-run the critique on the expanded SPL.
fragments.MID_SEARCH_TABLE: MID_SEARCH_TABLE (table in mid-pipeline; severity medium): table is transforming — it centralizes rows and drops fields mid-flight. Downstream commands then run on the SH against a format meant for display. Risk: Dropped fields silently break downstream lookups/evals that expected them. Fix: Use | fields to trim columns mid-pipeline (distributable); reserve table for the final display stage.
fragments.MID_TOKEN_WILDCARD: MID_TOKEN_WILDCARD (Mid-token wildcard across punctuation; severity high): Wildcards spanning punctuation (host=sh-*splunkcloud*) fight the segmenter: Splunk indexes segments split on punctuation, so matching costs more. Risk: Correctness hazard, not just cost — segment boundaries mean mid-token wildcards can silently match differently than intended. Fix: Match whole segments or use TERM() for exact tokens containing punctuation; split the filter into anchored parts.
fragments.MISSED_ALERT_WINDOWS: MISSED_ALERT_WINDOWS (Alert skipping evaluation windows; severity high): Cost is not the issue — coverage is. With realtime_schedule=1 (the default), a skipped run's time window is never evaluated at all. Risk: An alert with actions that has skipped runs has silent detection gaps: events in those windows were never inspected, and nothing tells the owner. The most dangerous failure mode a scheduled alert has. Fix: Set realtime_schedule=0 (continuous schedule) so missed windows are evaluated late rather than never; then fix the cause of the skips (self-overlap or scheduler pressure).
fragments.MISSING_FIELDS: MISSING_FIELDS (No early field trimming; severity low): Without | fields, every extracted column ships indexers → SH for every surviving event, whether or not anything downstream uses it. Risk: None — pure bandwidth/memory overhead. Fix: Add | fields keep-list immediately after retrieval (fields is distributable streaming, so it runs on the indexers).
fragments.MISSING_SOURCETYPE: MISSING_SOURCETYPE (Index without sourcetype scope; severity low): An index filter alone pulls every event class in that index; sourcetype narrows the lexicon walk and downstream field extraction. Risk: Extra event classes can also skew results (fields with the same name across sourcetypes). Fix: Add sourcetype= (and source=/host= where meaningful) to the retrieval stage.
fragments.MISSING_TERM_DIRECTIVE: MISSING_TERM_DIRECTIVE (Exact token without TERM(); severity medium): High-cardinality exact tokens containing minor segmenters (IPs, GUIDs) match faster as TERM(10.0.0.1) — one lexicon term instead of a segment intersection. Risk: Low risk; purely an efficiency opportunity. Fix: Wrap exact punctuated tokens in TERM(): TERM(10.0.0.1), TERM(user@host).
fragments.MULTIPLE_REX: MULTIPLE_REX (Sequential rex commands; severity low): Each rex re-reads the source field per event; several in sequence multiply parse passes that one combined pattern (or props-based extraction) would do once. Risk: Low — cost only. Fix: Combine into one rex with multiple named groups, or promote stable extractions into props.conf/transforms.conf.
fragments.MVEXPAND_MEMORY: MVEXPAND_MEMORY (mvexpand truncates at the memory cap; severity low): mvexpand holds the entire expanded chunk in search-head memory; carrying _raw along multiplies the footprint per output row. Risk: On overflow of max_mem_usage_mb (default 500 MB) mvexpand TRUNCATES the chunk and emits only a warning — the search succeeds with missing rows. Fix: Drop unused fields (especially _raw) before expanding: `... | fields - _raw | mvexpand <field>`, so the chunk stays under the cap.
fragments.NEAR_DUPLICATE: NEAR_DUPLICATE (One of several clones differing only in constants; severity medium): Other scheduled searches share this search's exact structure and differ only in literals (a threshold, a host, an index): the same scan runs once per clone, and the scheduler pays for each copy. Risk: Clones drift. A fix applied to one copy misses the others, and thresholds encoded as separate searches cannot be reviewed as one policy. Fix: Collapse the clones into one search that carries the varying value as a by-clause, a lookup, or a case expression, and alert on the aggregate.
fragments.NON_INDEXED_FILTER: NON_INDEXED_FILTER (Filtering on non-indexed form of an indexed field; severity medium): When an indexed (or default) field exists, filtering on the search-time equivalent forces _raw reads and extraction across more buckets. Risk: Low correctness risk; cost and latency only. Fix: Use the documented indexed field for the sourcetype (props.conf / CIM), or add an indexed term alongside the extracted-field filter.
fragments.NOT_STAR_UNPAREN: NOT_STAR_UNPAREN (Unparenthesized NOT *; severity high): Minor cost impact; this is primarily a correctness trap. Risk: NOT * combined with index= or other filters without parentheses evaluates with surprising precedence — wrong results, no error. Fix: Parenthesize: index=x (NOT *pattern*) — or better, replace the negation with an inclusion filter.
fragments.NO_SCHEDULE_COURTESY: NO_SCHEDULE_COURTESY (Frequent search without skew or schedule window; severity low): Non-alert reports that demand exact-time execution (allow_skew=0, no schedule_window) pile onto the same minute slots and crowd the scheduler — the thundering-herd ingredient. Risk: Contention it causes skips OTHER searches, including alerts. Fix: For reports that tolerate flexible timing: schedule_window=auto and/or allow_skew=5m; reserve exact-time slots for searches that need them.
fragments.OUTPUTLOOKUP_BLOAT: OUTPUTLOOKUP_BLOAT (outputlookup writes a bundle-replicated CSV; severity low): A CSV lookup table lives on the search head and is replicated to every indexer inside the knowledge bundle — and by default the whole table is re-sent each time any part of it changes. A large or frequently-written CSV bloats every search's bundle replication. (A KV Store target avoids this.) Risk: outputlookup is a flagged risky command (it can overwrite or lose data). Advisory: the CSV size is not visible in the SPL text, so this never blocks — most outputlookups are small and fine. Fix: For large or often-updated tables, write to a KV Store collection instead of a CSV (not bundle-replicated by default); keep CSV lookups small and rarely written; consider `override_if_empty=false` to avoid clobbering.
fragments.OVERRUN_RANGE: OVERRUN_RANGE (Runtime exceeds the time span searched; severity medium): The search spends more wall-clock running than the span of data it examines — e.g. it reads 5 minutes of events but takes 10 minutes to finish. A pure inefficiency signal: the work is dominated by how the search is written, not by how much time it covers. Risk: Runtime longer than the window makes self-overlap likely on any frequent schedule and wastes a scheduler slot for the whole duration. Fix: Fix the search structure (see its SPL findings — usually missing indexed filters, leading wildcards, or raw-data scans that tstats would answer); the window itself is fine, the search is slow for its size.
fragments.PHANTOM_INDEX: PHANTOM_INDEX (Reads only from indexes that do not exist here; severity high): Every literal index= in the retrieval stage names an index this instance does not define, so each scheduled run dispatches, opens nothing, returns nothing, and still spends a scheduler slot and a dispatch directory. Risk: The search looks healthy in every list (enabled, scheduled, succeeding) while it can never produce a result: a typo, a decommissioned index, or an app installed on the wrong tier hides a detection gap in plain sight. Fix: Point the search at the index that actually holds the data, or disable and remove it if that data was never onboarded here; audit the alert's consumers before deleting.
fragments.PREMATURE_TRANSFORM: PREMATURE_TRANSFORM (Transforming command before adequate filtering; severity medium): stats/sort/dedup are barriers: every event produced so far must arrive before they emit a row. Transforming the full candidate set then filtering the output wastes the whole difference. Risk: Barrier commands lengthen runDuration — scheduled searches drift toward self-overlap. Fix: Filter first: push search/where clauses before the transform; aggregate the smallest set that answers the question.
fragments.REALTIME_DISPATCH: REALTIME_DISPATCH (Real-time dispatch on a scheduled search; severity medium): A real-time dispatch window (rt- earliest / rt latest) runs a continuous search that holds a dedicated pipeline for as long as it lives — far more expensive than a periodic historical search, and it draws against the separate real-time search quota. Risk: "Scheduled" and "real-time" are contradictory intents: the search either runs continuously (pinning a slot the cron never releases) or its rt window is meaningless for a periodic run. Almost always a habit carried over from ad-hoc real-time searches, not a deliberate choice. Fix: Use historical relative-time bounds sized to the schedule (e.g. a */5 cron with earliest=-6m@m latest=now). If you truly need sub-second latency, an accelerated data model or an ingest-time pipeline scales where a standing real-time search does not.
fragments.SCAN_HEAVY_HISTORY: SCAN_HEAVY_HISTORY (Measured scan far broader than the answer; severity high): The _audit completion trail shows filtering efficiency below 5% with at least a thousand events scanned per run: historical proof, not a guess, that retrieval reads far more than the search keeps, on every run. Risk: Scan volume this far from the result set means the selective terms live after retrieval; as data grows the search slows toward its interval while its output stays the same. Fix: Move the selective filters into the retrieval stage (indexed fields, sourcetype, exact terms), or answer from tstats or a summary when only indexed fields are needed.
fragments.SELF_OVERLAP: SELF_OVERLAP (Runtime exceeds schedule interval; severity high): Average runtime longer than the cron interval means every run collides with the next — the search occupies its slot continuously. Risk: Guaranteed per-search max_concurrent skips: the schedule silently degrades to "whenever the previous run finishes". Fix: Make the search faster (see its SPL findings) or widen the interval to comfortably exceed p95 runtime.
fragments.SILENT_ALERT: SILENT_ALERT (Alert with actions that never fires; severity medium): Alert actions are wired, the search runs on schedule, and across the measured window no action ever fired: every run is a scan for a condition that does not match. Risk: A never-firing alert is indistinguishable from a broken one until the day it should have fired. Thresholds drift, field names change, sourcetypes get renamed; the alert stays green. Fix: Test the condition deliberately (inject a matching event or lower the threshold briefly) to prove the alert can fire, then decide whether the threshold is right or the alert should be retired.
fragments.SILENT_TRUNCATION: SILENT_TRUNCATION (Result set silently truncated; severity high): The cost is mostly already paid — this code is about the answer being wrong. Risk: Truncation at subsearch_maxout / maxresultrows produces confidently wrong results. In an alerting search this means missed detections, not slowness. Fix: Eliminate the pattern that can truncate (see JOIN_OVERUSE / SUBSEARCH_RISK rewrites); where a cap is genuinely acceptable, assert it explicitly with head and document why.
fragments.SORT_BEFORE_TRANSACTION: SORT_BEFORE_TRANSACTION (sort immediately before transaction; severity medium): sort is a full-dataset barrier stacked in front of the already-expensive transaction — two SH-bound buffering passes back to back. Risk: Usually a symptom: the author is fighting transaction's ordering requirement, a strong smell that stats is the right tool. Fix: Replace the pair with stats aggregation by the transaction key; if transaction is genuinely required, let it consume index order directly.
fragments.SORT_DEFAULT_LIMIT: SORT_DEFAULT_LIMIT (Unbounded sort truncates at 10,000; severity low): sort is a full-dataset barrier on the search head — the whole set is buffered before anything is emitted. Risk: A sort with no explicit count defaults to 10,000 results and silently discards the rest BEFORE downstream commands see them — a top-N over a larger set is computed on the wrong 10k, with no error. Harmless under 10k rows, wrong above it. Fix: State the bound: `sort 0 <field>` keeps everything (accepting the memory cost), `sort <N> <field>` takes an explicit top-N. Never rely on the implicit 10,000 default.
fragments.STARVED_SCHEDULE: STARVED_SCHEDULE (Chronically skipped at default priority; severity medium): The waste is inverted: a starved search barely consumes I/O because it is mostly being skipped. You are paying for a detection or report that rarely executes, and the slots it does win are spent losing races against the herd. Risk: Skipped far more often than it runs, due to scheduler contention rather than its own runtime, while sitting at default priority — so nothing will change: it keeps losing the slot lottery. Its alerts and reports silently do not fire, yet the search still looks enabled and healthy in the list. Fix: Decide whether the search matters. If it does, raise schedule_priority or move it off the contended minute (schedule_window=auto / allow_skew) so it stops colliding with the herd. If it does not, disable it. Either way, stop paying for a schedule that mostly never runs.
fragments.SUBSEARCH_EXPLOSION: SUBSEARCH_EXPLOSION (map with high maxsearches; severity high): map dispatches one search per input row (default cap 10). Raising maxsearches turns one query into a concurrent search storm competing for scheduler slots. Risk: Concurrency pressure skips OTHER searches — the blast radius is the whole scheduler, not this search. Fix: Restructure as a single search with a join key (stats by), a lookup, or a subsearch that feeds terms into one outer search.
fragments.SUBSEARCH_RISK: SUBSEARCH_RISK (Subsearch nearing platform caps; severity medium): Every subsearch is a full extra search dispatched before the outer one can proceed; the outer search blocks on it. Risk: Defaults: 60s timeout (subsearch_maxtime), 10k results (subsearch_maxout). Hitting either finalizes the subsearch early and the outer search runs on partial input — silently. Fix: Keep subsearches small and bounded (indexed filters, tight window); for large ID sets use lookups; for correlation use stats over a combined base search.
fragments.TRANSACTION_ABUSE: TRANSACTION_ABUSE (transaction at scale; severity high): transaction is centralized streaming: every candidate event is held in SH memory while transactions assemble. It also requires descending time order, defeating index-order streaming. Risk: At maxopentxn (5000) / maxopenevents (100k) Splunk evicts LRU transactions — results are silently incomplete. Docs and community agree: >90% of transaction uses are better served by stats. Fix: stats earliest(_time) AS start latest(_time) AS end values(...) BY id — add range(_time) for duration; reserve transaction for genuine startswith/endswith session semantics.
fragments.TRUNCATED_ALERT: TRUNCATED_ALERT (Alert payload capped below what the search produces; severity high): An explicit action.<name>.maxresults sits below the search's measured average results per run, so the delivered payload is a fraction of the matches; the scan is paid in full and most of the answer is discarded at the last step. Risk: Recipients see a partial list with no indication anything was dropped: the alert silently under-reports, and the missing rows are the ones that arrived last. Fix: Raise maxresults to cover the measured maximum, or aggregate in the search so the alert carries a summary instead of a truncated list.
fragments.TSTATS_DM_UNSCOPED: TSTATS_DM_UNSCOPED (tstats/datamodel without index scope; severity medium): tstats over an accelerated data model without index/sourcetype constraints scans all summary buckets — bloom-filter bucket elimination does not apply to DMA summaries the way it does to raw buckets. Risk: "It uses tstats so it is fast" is a false comfort at portfolio scale; these grow with the summary footprint. Fix: Constrain inside where: | tstats count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where nodename=All_Traffic index=fw by All_Traffic.action.
fragments.TSTATS_LOOKUP_WHERE: TSTATS_LOOKUP_WHERE (Expensive automatic lookup inside tstats where; severity medium): A where clause that can only be satisfied via an automatic lookup forces the full lookup to load and apply during what should be a tsidx-only operation. Risk: Cost only, but it silently converts the fast path into a slow one. Fix: Filter on model/indexed fields inside tstats; apply lookup enrichment and lookup-based filters after the tstats aggregation.
fragments.TSTATS_OPPORTUNITY: TSTATS_OPPORTUNITY (stats where tstats would serve; severity medium): Aggregating only indexed fields (index, sourcetype, source, host, _time) through raw-event stats reads _raw for nothing. tstats answers from tsidx alone — routinely 10-100x faster. Risk: None — opportunity, not hazard. (Semantics differ slightly: tstats counts from tsidx; validate parity when converting.) Fix: | tstats count where index=web by host — instead of index=web | stats count by host.
fragments.UNBOUNDED_INDEX: UNBOUNDED_INDEX (Unbounded index scan (index=*); severity critical): index=* scans every index: metadata explosion plus I/O across all buckets. Splunk treats it as a literal instruction to search everything, not a convenience default. Risk: Competes with every other search for IOPS and scheduler slots; on shared infrastructure a single index=* over a wide window can starve the cluster. Fix: Name the indexes that actually hold the data: index=web OR index=app. If the index is unknown, find it once with | eventcount summarize=false index=* or metadata, then pin it.
fragments.VERBOSE_MODE: VERBOSE_MODE (Verbose search mode where smart/fast suffices; severity low): Verbose mode extracts and returns every field and event even when the search only needs aggregates — pure overhead for reporting searches. Risk: None — cost only. Fix: Run reporting searches in smart or fast mode; verbose is for interactive exploration.
fragments.WINDOW_INTERVAL_MISMATCH: WINDOW_INTERVAL_MISMATCH (Dispatch window far exceeds schedule interval; severity high): A search that runs every 5 minutes over 24 hours of events re-scans the same data ~288 times a day — the window/interval ratio is a direct I/O multiplier on every run. Risk: Oversized windows push runDuration toward the cron interval (self-overlap skips) and usually signal copy-pasted dispatch settings nobody reviewed. Fix: Size the window to the interval plus a small safety overlap (e.g. */5 cron with earliest=-6m@m); for rolling aggregates use summary indexing instead of re-scanning history every run.
